questions.prompt: In an LU decomposition \(A=LU\), which factor is lower triangular and which is upper triangular?
questions.answer: The matrix \(L\) is lower triangular, meaning entries above its main diagonal are zero. The matrix \(U\) is upper triangular, meaning entries below its main diagonal are zero.

questions.prompt: Under the course convention, what entries appear on the diagonal of \(L\) in an LU decomposition?
questions.answer: Under the course convention, \(L\) has ones on its diagonal. This is often called a unit lower triangular factor.

questions.prompt: If \(A=LU\) and \(A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf b\), what two triangular systems are solved?
questions.answer: Write \(LU\mathbf{x}=\mathbf b\). Let \(\mathbf u=U\mathbf{x}\). First solve \(L\mathbf u=\mathbf b\) by forward substitution, then solve \(U\mathbf{x}=\mathbf u\) by backward substitution.

questions.prompt: Why is LU decomposition useful when many systems have the same coefficient matrix \(A\)?
questions.answer: Once \(A=LU\) is known, the same factors can be reused. Each new right-hand side only requires solving \(L\mathbf u=\mathbf b\) and \(U\mathbf{x}=\mathbf u\), which is faster than reducing the full matrix again.

questions.prompt: Solve \(L\mathbf u=\mathbf b\) for \(L=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\3&1\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\mathbf b=\begin{pmatrix}2\\11\end{pmatrix}\).
questions.answer: The equations are \(u_1=2\) and \(3u_1+u_2=11\). Substitute \(u_1=2\): \(6+u_2=11\), so \(u_2=5\). Therefore \[\mathbf u=\begin{pmatrix}2\\5\end{pmatrix}.\]

questions.prompt: Solve \(U\mathbf{x}=\mathbf u\) for \(U=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\0&3\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\mathbf u=\begin{pmatrix}7\\9\end{pmatrix}\).
questions.answer: The second row gives \(3x_2=9\), so \(x_2=3\). The first row gives \(2x_1+x_2=7\), so \(2x_1+3=7\), hence \(x_1=2\). Thus \[\mathbf{x}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\3\end{pmatrix}.\]

questions.prompt: Given \(L=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\2&1\end{pmatrix}\) and \(U=\begin{pmatrix}3&4\\0&5\end{pmatrix}\), compute \(A=LU\).
questions.answer: Multiply the factors: \[LU=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\2&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}3&4\\0&5\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}3&4\\6&13\end{pmatrix}.\] Therefore \(A=\begin{pmatrix}3&4\\6&13\end{pmatrix}\).

questions.prompt: For \(A=LU\), solve using \(L=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\4&1\end{pmatrix}\), \(U=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\0&3\end{pmatrix}\), and \(\mathbf b=\begin{pmatrix}5\\23\end{pmatrix}\).
questions.answer: First solve \(L\mathbf u=\mathbf b\): \(u_1=5\) and \(4u_1+u_2=23\), so \(20+u_2=23\) and \(u_2=3\). Now solve \(U\mathbf{x}=\mathbf u\): \(3x_2=3\), so \(x_2=1\). Then \(2x_1+x_2=5\), so \(2x_1=4\) and \(x_1=2\). Hence \[\mathbf{x}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\end{pmatrix}.\]

questions.prompt: Solve \(A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf b\) for \(A=LU\), where \(L=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\2&1&0\\-1&3&1\end{pmatrix}\), \(U=\begin{pmatrix}2&1&0\\0&1&4\\0&0&3\end{pmatrix}\), and \(\mathbf b=\begin{pmatrix}2\\5\\10\end{pmatrix}\).
questions.answer: First solve \(L\mathbf u=\mathbf b\). The equations are \(u_1=2\), \(2u_1+u_2=5\), and \(-u_1+3u_2+u_3=10\). Thus \(u_2=1\) and \(u_3=9\). Now solve \(U\mathbf{x}=\mathbf u\): \(3x_3=9\), so \(x_3=3\). Then \(x_2+4x_3=1\), so \(x_2=-11\). Finally \(2x_1+x_2=2\), so \(2x_1=13\) and \(x_1=\frac{13}{2}\).

questions.prompt: Find an LU decomposition with unit diagonal \(L\) for \(A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\6&5\end{pmatrix}\).
questions.answer: Eliminate the entry below the first pivot: the multiplier is \(6/2=3\). Thus \(L=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\3&1\end{pmatrix}\). The row operation \(R_2\leftarrow R_2-3R_1\) gives \(U=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\0&2\end{pmatrix}\). Check: \[LU=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\3&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\0&2\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\6&5\end{pmatrix}.\]

questions.prompt: Explain why forward substitution is used before backward substitution in an LU solve.
questions.answer: Since \(A=LU\), the equation is \(LU\mathbf{x}=\mathbf b\). The vector closest to \(\mathbf b\) is \(\mathbf u=U\mathbf{x}\), so the first system is \(L\mathbf u=\mathbf b\). Because \(L\) is lower triangular, this is solved from top to bottom by forward substitution. Only after \(\mathbf u\) is known can \(U\mathbf{x}=\mathbf u\) be solved from bottom to top.

questions.prompt: A student solves \(U\mathbf{x}=\mathbf b\) first when \(A=LU\). Explain the mistake.
questions.answer: The equation is \(LU\mathbf{x}=\mathbf b\), not \(U\mathbf{x}=\mathbf b\). The product \(U\mathbf{x}\) equals the intermediate vector \(\mathbf u\), and \(L\mathbf u=\mathbf b\). Solving \(U\mathbf{x}=\mathbf b\) ignores the effect of \(L\), so it generally gives the wrong \(\mathbf{x}\).

questions.prompt: Find a unit-diagonal LU decomposition for \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&0\\3&7&1\\2&5&4\end{pmatrix}\).
questions.answer: Use the first pivot \(1\). The multipliers are \(3\) and \(2\), so eliminate with \(R_2-3R_1\) and \(R_3-2R_1\), giving rows \([0,1,1]\) and \([0,1,4]\). Use the second pivot \(1\) with multiplier \(1\), so \(R_3\leftarrow R_3-R_2\), giving \([0,0,3]\). Thus \[U=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&0\\0&1&1\\0&0&3\end{pmatrix},\quad L=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\3&1&0\\2&1&1\end{pmatrix}.\]

questions.prompt: Use the LU factors from \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&0\\3&7&1\\2&5&4\end{pmatrix}\), \(L=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\3&1&0\\2&1&1\end{pmatrix}\), \(U=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&0\\0&1&1\\0&0&3\end{pmatrix}\), to solve \(A\mathbf{x}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\5\\8\end{pmatrix}\).
questions.answer: First solve \(L\mathbf u=\mathbf b\). The equations are \(u_1=1\), \(3u_1+u_2=5\), and \(2u_1+u_2+u_3=8\). Thus \(u_2=2\) and \(u_3=4\). Now solve \(U\mathbf{x}=\mathbf u\): \(3x_3=4\), so \(x_3=\frac43\). Then \(x_2+x_3=2\), so \(x_2=\frac23\). Finally \(x_1+2x_2=1\), so \(x_1=-\frac13\).

questions.prompt: For \(A=\begin{pmatrix}a&1\\2&3\end{pmatrix}\), identify when a no-row-swap LU decomposition using the first pivot fails.
questions.answer: A no-row-swap LU decomposition starts with the first pivot \(a\). The multiplier below it is \(2/a\), so this step requires \(a\ne0\). If \(a=0\), the first pivot is zero and the method fails without a row swap. Thus the no-row-swap first-pivot LU process fails at the first step when \(a=0\).

questions.prompt: For \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&k\\2&4\end{pmatrix}\), find when the second pivot in no-row-swap LU is zero.
questions.answer: Use the first pivot \(1\). The multiplier is \(2\), so the second row becomes \([2,4]-2[1,k]=[0,4-2k]\). The second pivot is \(4-2k\). It is zero when \(4-2k=0\), so \(k=2\).

questions.prompt: A single LU factorisation of \(A\) is used to solve two systems with right-hand sides \(\mathbf b_1\) and \(\mathbf b_2\). Describe exactly what work is reused and what work must be repeated.
questions.answer: The expensive factorisation \(A=LU\) is reused. For each right-hand side, the triangular solves must be repeated: solve \(L\mathbf u_1=\mathbf b_1\), then \(U\mathbf{x}_1=\mathbf u_1\); solve \(L\mathbf u_2=\mathbf b_2\), then \(U\mathbf{x}_2=\mathbf u_2\). The factors \(L\) and \(U\) stay the same, but the intermediate vectors and final solutions change.

questions.prompt: Diagnose this error: "Since \(A=LU\), we may set \(\mathbf u=L\mathbf{x}\) and solve \(U\mathbf u=\mathbf b\)."
questions.answer: The grouping is wrong. From \(A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf b\) and \(A=LU\), we have \(L(U\mathbf{x})=\mathbf b\). The natural intermediate vector is \(\mathbf u=U\mathbf{x}\), not \(L\mathbf{x}\). Then the systems are \(L\mathbf u=\mathbf b\) and \(U\mathbf{x}=\mathbf u\). Reversing this order changes the equation and generally gives a wrong solution.

questions.prompt: Explain why zero pivots matter in LU decomposition even if the original system might still be solvable.
questions.answer: A no-row-swap LU process divides by pivots to form elimination multipliers. If a required pivot is zero, that multiplier is undefined, so the particular factorisation process stops. The original system may still be solvable after swapping rows or using another method, but the no-row-swap LU decomposition with unit diagonal \(L\) is not available in that form.

questions.prompt: Show why \(A=LU\) with triangular factors makes solving easier than multiplying out \(A\) and row-reducing from scratch each time.
questions.answer: Once \(A=LU\) is known, solving \(A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf b\) becomes two structured solves. The lower triangular system \(L\mathbf u=\mathbf b\) determines one unknown at a time from top to bottom. The upper triangular system \(U\mathbf{x}=\mathbf u\) determines one unknown at a time from bottom to top. This avoids repeating the full elimination of \(A\) for every new \(\mathbf b\), so repeated solves become simpler and more reliable.
